shortQuestions: Nucleophilic substitution: an electron-rich nucleophile (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃) attacks an electron-deficient carbon and replaces a leaving group, e.g. CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻; typical of alkyl halides; mechanisms SN1 and SN2.

Electrophilic substitution: an electron-deficient electrophile (NO₂⁺, Br⁺, R⁺) attacks the electron-rich π cloud of an aromatic ring and replaces a hydrogen via an arenium ion, e.g. C₆H₆ + NO₂⁺ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H⁺; typical of benzene.
In an alkyl halide the C–X bond is polar (Cδ+–Xδ−): the carbon is electron-deficient, so it attracts nucleophiles, and X⁻ is a good leaving group.

Benzene has an electron-rich delocalised π cloud that repels nucleophiles but attracts electrophiles; substitution of an H (rather than addition) keeps the stable aromatic ring intact. So benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution.
A tertiary carbocation R₃C⁺ has three alkyl groups attached to the positive carbon.
Alkyl groups release electrons (+I effect) and stabilise the charge by hyperconjugation (overlap of C–H σ bonds with the empty p orbital), spreading out the positive charge.
More alkyl groups mean more stabilisation: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺.
SN1 and E1 have the same slow (rate-determining) step: ionisation of the tertiary alkyl halide into a carbocation, favoured by the polar protic solvent: R–X → R⁺ + X⁻.

Both rates are therefore rate = k[RX] with the same k. Afterwards the carbocation either combines with a nucleophile (SN1) or loses a β-proton (E1) in fast steps, which decide only the product ratio, not the rate.

In a polar protic solvent (water, alcohol) the small, highly charged F⁻ is strongly hydrogen-bonded and surrounded by solvent molecules, so its lone pairs are not available — it is a weak nucleophile.
In a polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, acetone, DMF) anions are poorly solvated; F⁻ is 'naked', highly reactive and becomes a strong nucleophile.
In SN2 the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite to the leaving group (backside attack).
This avoids repulsion between the electron-rich nucleophile and the electron-rich leaving group, and lets the nucleophile overlap with the large back lobe of the C–X σ* orbital.
The three other groups flip over like an umbrella in a wind, so the configuration is inverted (Walden inversion).
Reactivity depends on C–X bond strength and the stability of the leaving halide ion.
C–F is the strongest bond (≈ 485 kJ mol⁻¹) and F⁻ a poor leaving group, so alkyl fluorides are least reactive.
C–I is the weakest (≈ 240 kJ mol⁻¹) and the large, polarisable I⁻ is the best leaving group, so alkyl iodides are most reactive.
In the gas phase basicity follows the +I effect: 3° > 2° > 1°. In water the protonated amine is stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water.
R₂NH₂⁺ (from a secondary amine) has two N–H bonds to hydrogen-bond with water, but R₃NH⁺ has only one; tertiary amines are also more crowded around nitrogen.
Poorer solvation of R₃NH⁺ makes tertiary amines weaker bases than secondary amines in aqueous solution.
In CH₃⁺ the carbon forms only three σ bonds and has no lone pair; it is sp²-hybridised.

The three bonding pairs repel equally and lie in one plane at 120° (trigonal planar), with an empty p orbital perpendicular to the plane. A pyramidal shape would require a fourth electron pair (as in a carbanion).
A nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient carbon; nucleophilicity is a kinetic property (rate of attack).
A base donates an electron pair to a proton (H⁺); basicity is a thermodynamic property (position of equilibrium).
Every nucleophile is a Lewis base, but strength can differ: I⁻ is a good nucleophile but a weak base; (CH₃)₃CO⁻ is a strong base but a poor nucleophile (bulky).
longQuestions: (a) Preparation of alkyl halides: (i) From alcohols with hydrogen halides: ROH + HX → RX + H₂O (HCl needs ZnCl₂, Lucas reagent). (ii) From alcohols with phosphorus halides: ROH + PCl₅ → RCl + POCl₃ + HCl; 3ROH + PBr₃ → 3RBr + H₃PO₃. (iii) With thionyl chloride (best, gaseous by-products): ROH + SOCl₂ —pyridine→ RCl + SO₂ + HCl. (iv) Addition of HX to alkenes (Markovnikov): CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃. (v) Free-radical halogenation of alkanes: CH₄ + Cl₂ —UV→ CH₃Cl + HCl. (vi) Halide exchange (Finkelstein): RCl + NaI —acetone→ RI + NaCl.

(b) Elimination (β-elimination, dehydrohalogenation): heating an alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH removes H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon to give an alkene: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O.

E2: one-step, concerted; the base removes the β-H as X leaves; rate = k[RX][base]; favoured by strong bases and requires anti-periplanar H and X. E1: two steps via a carbocation (slow ionisation, then loss of H⁺); rate = k[RX]; favoured by tertiary halides and polar protic solvents.
Saytzeff's rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product, e.g. 2-bromobutane gives mainly but-2-ene.

(a) SN1 (unimolecular): Step 1 (slow): R₃C–X → R₃C⁺ + X⁻. Step 2 (fast): R₃C⁺ + Nu⁻ → R₃C–Nu. Rate = k[RX] (first order). The planar carbocation is attacked from either side, giving racemisation. Favoured by 3° halides, polar protic solvents and weak nucleophiles; rearrangements may occur.

SN2 (bimolecular): one step — the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the back while X leaves, through a transition state [Nu···C···X]⁻ with five groups around carbon. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order). Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion). Favoured by methyl and 1° halides, strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents; hindered by bulky groups.

(b)(i) Substrate: the molecule on which a reagent acts, e.g. the alkyl halide in a substitution reaction. (ii) Leaving group: the atom or group that departs from the substrate taking the bonding electron pair, e.g. Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻; good leaving groups are weak bases. (iii) Carbocation: an ion in which a carbon atom has only six valence electrons and a positive charge, bonded to three groups; sp²-hybridised and planar, e.g. (CH₃)₃C⁺.

(a) Preparation: an alkyl (or aryl) halide is added to magnesium turnings in dry (anhydrous) ether: R–X + Mg —dry ether→ R–Mg–X (e.g. CH₃I + Mg → CH₃MgI). Moisture must be excluded because water destroys the reagent (RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X).
(b)(i) Aldehydes: formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol and other aldehydes give secondary alcohols. HCHO + CH₃MgI → CH₃CH₂OMgI → (H₃O⁺) CH₃CH₂OH; CH₃CHO + CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₂CHOMgI → (CH₃)₂CHOH.
(ii) Ketones give tertiary alcohols: (CH₃)₂CO + CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₃COMgI → (H₃O⁺) (CH₃)₃COH.
(iii) Esters react with two moles to give tertiary alcohols: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃MgI → CH₃COCH₃ (ketone) + C₂H₅OMgI; CH₃COCH₃ + CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₃COMgI → (CH₃)₃COH.
(iv) Carbon dioxide gives carboxylic acids: RMgX + CO₂ → RCOOMgX → (H₃O⁺) RCOOH, e.g. CH₃MgI → CH₃COOH.

(a) Preparation of amines: (i) Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: RX + NH₃ → RNH₂ + HX (excess RX gives R₂NH, R₃N and R₄N⁺X⁻). (ii) Reduction of nitriles: RC≡N + 4[H] —LiAlH₄ or Na/C₂H₅OH→ RCH₂NH₂. (iii) Reduction of nitro compounds: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] —Sn/HCl→ C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O. (iv) Reduction of amides with LiAlH₄; Hofmann degradation: RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → RNH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O.
Structure: nitrogen is sp³-hybridised; three σ bonds and a lone pair give a pyramidal shape with C–N–C angles of about 108°.

Basicity: the lone pair on N accepts a proton: RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia (+I effect of alkyl groups); in water the order is 2° > 1° ≈ 3° > NH₃. Aromatic amines (aniline) are weaker bases because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring.

(b) Reactions of amines: (i) with acids → salts: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻. (ii) Alkylation with RX → 2°, 3° amines and quaternary salts. (iii) Acylation: CH₃NH₂ + CH₃COCl → CH₃NHCOCH₃ + HCl. (iv) With nitrous acid: 1° aliphatic amines give alcohols and N₂ gas; aromatic 1° amines give diazonium salts at 0–5 °C (C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O). (v) Carbylamine test: RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → RNC (foul-smelling isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H₂O. (vi) Hinsberg test with benzenesulphonyl chloride.

(a) Carbocations are positively charged carbon species in which the carbon has six valence electrons and three bonds; they are sp²-hybridised and planar. Formation: (i) heterolysis of an alkyl halide in a polar solvent: (CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻; (ii) protonation of an alkene: CH₂=CH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺; (iii) protonation of an alcohol followed by loss of water: (CH₃)₃COH + H⁺ → (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺ → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + H₂O.

(b) Stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl (3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺). Alkyl groups donate electrons by the inductive effect and by hyperconjugation, dispersing the positive charge; more alkyl groups mean greater stability. Allylic and benzylic carbocations are especially stable because of resonance.

(c, d) Structural formulas: i. 3-methylpentane-2,3-diamine: CH₃–CH(NH₂)–C(CH₃)(NH₂)–CH₂–CH₃. ii. 2,3-dimethylhexane-2,3-diamine: (CH₃)₂C(NH₂)–C(CH₃)(NH₂)–CH₂CH₂CH₃. iii. 2-bromo-3-fluoro-2,3-dimethylpentane: (CH₃)₂CBr–CF(CH₃)–CH₂CH₃.

iv. 4-bromo-4-chloro-3-fluoro-2,3-dimethylhexane: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CF(CH₃)–CBrCl–CH₂CH₃. v. 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylpentan-2-amine: CH₃–CCl(NH₂)–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂CH₃. (Part (c) prints no structures to be named, so only part (d) can be answered.)
activities: Primary amine: reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to give an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide that still has an acidic N–H; it dissolves in NaOH as its sodium salt, so a single clear layer is seen. C₆H₅SO₂Cl + RNH₂ → C₆H₅SO₂NHR + HCl; C₆H₅SO₂NHR + NaOH → C₆H₅SO₂N⁻R Na⁺ + H₂O. Acidifying precipitates the sulphonamide.
Secondary amine: gives an N,N-dialkylsulphonamide C₆H₅SO₂NR₂ with no N–H; it is insoluble in NaOH, so two layers form, and the organic layer is also insoluble in dilute HCl.
Tertiary amine: has no N–H and does not form a sulphonamide; it stays as a separate layer in NaOH but dissolves in 5% HCl because it forms a soluble ammonium salt (R₃NH⁺Cl⁻).
So: one layer → primary; layer insoluble in both NaOH and HCl → secondary; layer soluble in HCl → tertiary.
